category_title: Friendly, talkative boys who struggle to focus during independent reading
minimal_context: The student is participating in a classroom reading period with the goal of reading an assigned text.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time for our independent reading period. Please open your assigned text and begin reading.

STUDENT: Do we really have to read this one? Honestly, reading this just feels like a chore.

TUTOR: Yes, please focus on the assigned reading for now.

STUDENT: I can't focus on it. With all the pressures and problems I've got going on, reading this is an impossibility.

TUTOR: Just do your best to keep trying with the assigned text.

STUDENT: (Resists the teacher's direction and quietly hides a copy of The Bully under his assigned text so he can read that instead)

options.A: Use survey data to cater to the student's interests by bringing nonfiction and popular culture into the classroom, such as articles about Chris Brown, Reggaeton, and the New York Yankees.
options.B: Adopt a 'presumption-of-competence' stance, listen for counter-narratives during the independent reading period, and leverage teacher authority to 'fix' the interactional protocol rather than 'fixing' the student.
options.C: Implement an in-class reward system during the independent reading period where whenever the student accomplishes the day's reading target, they earn a sticker for their chart.
options.D: Use a character's weakness from the assigned text as a metaphor to engage in dialogue about what wasn't supposed to be talked about, such as the 'disabilities' listed in their IEP.
